The mustard plant with knobby, fist-sized, swollen green stem is known as "big-stem mustard" or "swollen-stem mustard". |} == Uses == === Nutrition === {{nutritionalvalue | name=Mustard greens, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt | kJ=110 | water=92 g | protein=2.56 g | fat=0.47 g | carbs=4.51 g | fiber=2 g | sugars=1.41 g | calcium_mg=118 | iron_mg=0.87 | magnesium_mg=13 | phosphorus_mg=42 | potassium_mg=162 | sodium_mg=9 | zinc_mg=0.22 | vitC_mg=25.3 | thiamin_mg=0.041 | riboflavin_mg=0.063 | niacin_mg=0.433 | pantothenic_mg=0.12 | vitB6_mg=0.098 | folate_ug=9 | vitA_ug=618 | betacarotene_ug=7400 | lutein_ug=10400 | vitE_mg=1.78 | vitK_ug=592.7 | source_usda = 1 | note=[https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/food-details/169257/nutrients Full Link to USDA Database entry] }} In a {{convert|100|g|oz|frac=2|abbr=off|adj=on}} reference serving, cooked mustard greens provide {{convert|26|kcal|kJ|order=flip|abbr=off}} of [[food energy]] and are a rich source (20% or more of the [[Daily Value]]) of vitamins [[vitamin A|A]], [[vitamin C|C]], and [[vitamin K|K]]—K being especially high as a multiple of its Daily Value. Mustard greens are a moderate source of [[vitamin E]] and [[calcium]]. Greens are 92% water, 4.5% [[carbohydrate]]s, 2.6% [[protein (nutrient)|protein]] and 0.5% [[fat]] (table). === Cuisine === [[File:Takanaduke1.jpg|thumb|Japanese ''takana'']] The leaves, seeds, and stems of this mustard variety are edible. The plant appears in some form in [[African cuisine|African]], [[Bangladeshi cuisine|Bangladeshi]], [[Chinese cuisine|Chinese]], [[Filipino cuisine|Filipino]], [[Tripuri cuisine|Tripuri]], [[Italian cuisine|Italian]], [[Indian cuisine|Indian]], [[Japanese cuisine|Japanese]], [[Okinawan cuisine|Okinawan]], [[Nepali cuisine|Nepali]], [[Pakistani]], [[Korean cuisine|Korean]], [[Southern American cuisine|Southern]], [[Taiwanese cuisine|Taiwanese]], and [[African-American cuisine|African-American]] (soul food) cuisines. Cultivars of ''B. juncea'' are grown for their [[greens (vegetable)|greens]], and for the production of [[mustard oil]]. The mustard condiment made from the seeds of the ''B. juncea'' is called brown mustard and is considered to be [[pungency|spicier]] than yellow mustard.{{cite journal|last1=Sakorn |first1=P.|last2=Rakariyatham |first2=N. |title=Biodegradation of glucosinolates in brown mustard seed meal (Brassica juncea) by Aspergillus sp. NR-4201 in liquid and solid-state cultures.|journal=Biodegradation|date=June 13, 2012|pmid=12713131|volume=13|issue=6|pages=395–9|doi=10.1023/A:1022851129684|s2cid=23927681}}{{cite book |last1=Polistico |first1=Edgie |title=Philippine Food, Cooking, & Dining Dictionary |date=2017 |publisher=Anvil Publishing, Inc. |isbn=9786214200870}} Because it may contain [[erucic acid]], a potential [[toxin]], mustard oil is restricted from import as a [[vegetable oil]] into the United States.{{cite web|url=https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cms_ia/importalert_89.html|title=Detention Without Physical Examination of Expressed Mustard Oil|publisher=US Food and Drug Administration|date=18 March 2011|access-date=1 February 2016|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303021049/http://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cms_ia/importalert_89.html|archive-date=3 March 2016}} [[Essential oil]] of mustard, however, is [[generally recognized as safe]] by the U.S. [[Food and Drug Administration]]. In [[Russia]], this is the main species grown for the production of [[mustard oil]]. It is widely used in [[canning]], [[baking]] and [[margarine]] production in Russia, and the majority of Russian [[mustard (condiment)|table mustard]] is also made from ''B. juncea''. The leaves are used in African cooking,Grubben, G.J.H. & Denton, O.A. (2004) Plant Resources of Tropical Africa 2. Vegetables. PROTA Foundation, Wageningen; Backhuys, Leiden; CTA, Wageningen. and all plant parts are used in [[Nepali cuisine]], particularly in the mountain regions of [[Nepal]], as well as in the [[Punjabi cuisine]] in the northern part of the [[Indian subcontinent]], where a dish called ''[[Sarson Da Saag|sarson da saag]]'' (mustard greens) is prepared.{{cite news|last=Chandrassekaran|first=V. K.|title=Flavour of Punjab|url=http://www.thehindu.com/features/metroplus/flavour-of-punjab/article4446215.ece|access-date=6 March 2013|newspaper=The Hindu|date=February 24, 2013|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130227010811/http://www.thehindu.com/features/metroplus/flavour-of-punjab/article4446215.ece|archive-date=27 February 2013}} ''B. juncea'' subsp. ''tatsai'', which has a particularly thick stem, is used to make the [[Nepali pickle]] called ''achar'', and the [[Chinese pickles|Chinese pickled products]] ''[[zha cai]]''. This plant is called "lai xaak" in Assamese and it is cultivated hugely during the winters. It is eaten in any form in Assam and Northeast, be it boiled or added raw in salad, cooked alone or with pork. During [[Taiwanese New Year]]'s Eve, [[Taiwan]]ese people eat mustard green ({{zh|t=長年菜|p=cháng nián cài}}) as a part of the reunion dinner, symbolizing longevity.{{Cite news|url=https://www.chinatimes.com/realtimenews/20240211000540-260418?chdtv|title=不只抗癌又護神經 專家曝「長年菜」5大好處 1招降苦味|language=zh-tw|author=郭冀銘|work=[[China Times]]|access-date=7 January 2025|date=2024-02-11}}{{Cite news|url=https://health.udn.com/health/story/6037/7761647|title=降血壓、保眼護膚又助抗癌 年菜必備「長年菜」芥菜營養價值高|language=zh-tw|author=黃妙雲|work=[[United Daily News]]|access-date=7 January 2025|date=2024-02-07}} The [[Gorkhas]] of the [[Indian states]] of [[Darjeeling]], West Bengal and [[Sikkim]] as well as [[Nepal]] prepare pork with mustard greens (also called ''rayo'' in [[Nepali language|Nepali]]). It is usually eaten with relish and steamed rice, but can also be eaten with ''[[roti]]'' ([[griddle]] breads). In Nepal it is also a common practice to cook these greens with meat of all sorts, especially goat meat; which is normally prepared in a pressure cooker with minimal use of spices to focus on the flavour of the greens and dry chillies. ''B. juncea'' (especially the seeds) is more pungent than greens from the closely related ''[[Brassica oleracea|B. oleracea]]'' ([[kale]], [[broccoli]], and [[collard greens]]),{{cite journal|pmid=25156799|year=2014|last1=Ghawi|first1=S. K.|title=Consumer acceptability and sensory profile of cooked broccoli with mustard seeds added to improve chemoprotective properties|journal=Journal of Food Science|volume=79|issue=9|pages=S1756–62|last2=Shen|first2=Y|last3=Niranjan|first3=K|last4=Methven|first4=L|doi=10.1111/1750-3841.12556}} and is frequently mixed with these milder greens in a dish of "mixed greens". [[Cuisine of China|Chinese]] and [[Japanese cuisine]]s also make use of mustard greens. In Japanese cuisine, it is known as ''takana'' and often pickled for use as filling in [[onigiri]] or as a condiment. Many varieties of ''B. juncea'' cultivars are used, including ''zha cai'', ''[[mizuna]]'', ''takana'' (var. ''integrifolia''), ''juk gai choy'', and ''xuelihong''. Asian mustard greens are most often [[stir-fry|stir-fried]] or [[pickled]]. (See [[pickled mustard]].) A [[Southeast Asian cuisine|Southeast Asian]] dish called ''asam gai choy'' or ''kiam chai boey'' is often made with leftovers from a large meal. It involves stewing mustard greens with [[tamarind]], dried [[chillies]] and leftover meat on the bone. Brassica juncea is also known as ''gai choi'', ''siu gai choi'', ''xiao jie cai'', baby mustard, Chinese leaf mustard or ''mostaza''.{{cite web|url=http://www.cherryfarms.co.uk/kaichoi.html|title=Kai Anjum|title=The plant family Brassicaceae contribution towards phytoremediation|date=2012|publisher=Springer|location=Dordrecht|isbn=9789400739130|display-editors=etal}} In particular, ''B. juncea'' was particularly effective at removing [[cadmium]] from soil.{{cite journal|last1=Schneider|first1=Thorsten|last2=Haag-Kerwer|first2=Angela|last3=Maetz|first3=Mischa|last4=Niecke|first4=Manfred|last5=Povh|first5=Bogdan|last6=Rausch|first6=Thomas|last7=Schüßler|first7=Arthur|title=Micro-PIXE studies of elemental distribution in Cd-accumulating Brassica juncea L|journal=Nuclear Instruments and Methods in Physics Research Section B: Beam Interactions with Materials and Atoms|date=September 1999|volume=158|issue=1–4|pages=329–334|doi=10.1016/S0168-583X(99)00356-0|bibcode=1999NIMPB.158..329S}} The process of removing heavy metals ends when the plant is harvested and properly discarded. Phytoremediation has been shown to be cheaper and easier than traditional methods for heavy metal reduction in soils.{{Cite journal |pmc=2266886 |title=Phytoremediation of heavy metal polluted soils and water: Progresses and perspectives|journal=Journal of Zhejiang University Science B|volume=9|issue=3|pages=210–220|year=2008|last1=Lone|first1=M. I|last2=He|first2=Z. L|last3=Stoffella|first3=P. J|last4=Yang|first4=X. E|doi=10.1631/jzus.B0710633|pmid=18357623}} In addition, it has the effect of reducing soil erosion, reducing cross-site contamination. == See also == *''[[Sinapis alba]]'' (formerly ''Brassica alba'') – yellow or [[white mustard]], another mustard variety *''[[Brassica oleracea]]'' – wild cabbage *''[[Brassica nigra]]'' – black mustard, another mustard variety *''[[Brassica rapa]]'' – related family of edible greens used in Asian cooking *''[[Brassica carinata]]'' – Ethiopian mustard *For other edible plants in the family [[Brassicaceae]], see [[cruciferous vegetables]]. == References == {{Reflist}} == Further reading == {{Scholia|topic}} * {{cite book |last1=Everitt |first1=J.H. |last2=Lonard |first2=R.L. |last3=Little |first3=C.R. |title=Weeds in South Texas and Northern Mexico |publisher=Texas Tech University Press |location=Lubbock |year=2007}} {{ISBN|0-89672-614-2}}. == External links == * [https://web.archive.org/web/20120314051507/http://database.prota.org/dbtw-wpd/exec/dbtwpub.dll?AC=QBE_QUERY&BU=http%3A%2F%2Fdatabase.prota.org%2Fsearch.htm&TN=PROTAB~1&QB0=AND&QF0=Species+Code&QI0=Brassica+juncea&RF=Webdisplay PROTAbase on ''Brassica juncea''] * [http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/duke_energy/Brassica_juncea.html Brassica juncea] {{unimelb|Brassica_juncea.html}} * [https://web.archive.org/web/20140327090145/http://cru.cahe.wsu.edu/CEPublications/eb1952e/EB1952E.pdf Mustard Green Manures: Washington State University Extension paper on cover crops.] * {{PFAF|Brassica juncea}} {{Herbs & spices}} {{Brassica}} {{Taxonbar|from=Q504781}} {{Authority control}} [[Category:Asian vegetables]] [[Category:Brassica|juncea]] [[Category:East Asian cuisine]] [[Category:South Asian cuisine]] [[Category:African cuisine]] [[Category:African-American cuisine]] [[Category:South American cuisine]] [[Category:Leaf vegetables]] [[Category:Phytoremediation plants]]
